q: 1. According to Hook's law, which one is wrong?
explain: Hooke's Law states Stress = E × Strain. Therefore, MoE × Stress = Strain is mathematically incorrect.

q: 2. The property of a material by which it can be beaten or rolled into thin plates, is called
explain: Malleability is the property that allows a material to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets, typically under compressive forces.

q: 3. The percentage reduction of a material from a direct compressive test indicates
explain: Similar to elongation in tension, reduction in cross-sectional area in compression is a measure of ductility.

q: 4. The impact tests are used to determine
explain: Tests like Charpy and Izod measure the energy absorbed during impact, which defines the toughness.

q: 5. Simple bending equation is
explain: This is the standard Euler-Bernoulli bending equation relating moment, inertia, stress, and curvature.

q: 6. In a composite bar the load distribution among different materials of which it is made is based on the assumption the all the materials will have
explain: In composite bars, the primary assumption for compatibility is that all components undergo the same amount of strain.

q: 7. The maximum strain energy stored in a specimen when strained within the elastic limit is known as
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum energy that can be stored without causing permanent deformation.

q: 8. Find the elongation of a rod if a load of p is applied on a rod having length, l c/s area, A and modulus of elasticity, E
explain: The standard formula for axial deformation is derived from Hooke's Law (σ = Eε), where strain ε = Δl/l and stress σ = p/A.

q: 9. The amount of stress developed due to increase in temperature in case of SSB if l=10m, ΔT=10°C, A=5cm²
explain: As per key 1 but In a Simply Supported Beam (SSB), the beam is free to expand or contract. Since there is no restriction to thermal expansion, no thermal stress is developed.

q: 10. A member having cross section 5 cm × 5 cm is subjected to a tensile stress of 100 kg/cm², then the applied load should be
explain: Load = Stress × Area. Area = 5cm × 5cm = 25cm². Load = 100 kg/cm² × 25cm² = 2500 kg.

q: 11. In a case of partially elastic body that part of work done by the external forces during deformation is dissipated in the form of heat, which is developed in the body during
explain: In a partially elastic body, the energy lost as heat corresponds to the non-elastic (permanent/plastic) portion of deformation, since elastic deformation energy is fully recoverable.

q: 12. Buckling load for a given column depends upon
options: both length and least lateral dimension
explain: Euler's buckling load formula (P = π²EI/Le²) depends on both the effective length of the column and the moment of inertia (related to the least lateral dimension).

q: 13. The maximum shear stress from a Mohr's circle is given by
options: the distance of centre from the origin
the distance of farthest point on the mohr's circle from origin
explain: On Mohr's circle, the vertical extent (top or bottom point) represents the maximum shear stress, which equals the radius of the circle.

q: 14. Stress may be expressed in Newton's
explain: In engineering practice (especially for structural/mechanical stresses), stress is conventionally expressed in N/mm² (MPa) due to convenient magnitude.

q: 15. To ascertain the maximum permissible eccentricity of loads on circular columns, the rule generally followed, is
explain: The 'middle third rule' states that a load must be kept within the middle third of the section width/diameter to avoid tension, which is the generally followed rule for columns.

q: 16. The deformation of a spring produced by a unit load is called
explain: Flexibility is defined as the deformation produced by a unit load, the reciprocal of stiffness.

q: 17. The maximum magnitude of shear stress due to shear force F on a rectangular section area A at the neutral axis is
explain: For a rectangular section, the parabolic shear stress distribution peaks at the neutral axis with a value of 1.5 times the average shear stress (F/A), giving 3F/2A.

q: 18. The stress along the contact surface of a rivet and the member is
explain: The stress developed at the contact/bearing surface between two members (e.g., a pin and a plate, or a column base on a footing) is termed bearing stress.

q: 19. In a stressed body the minimum normal stress at any point is always
options: average of two normal stresses acting in the two principal directions
difference of two normal stresses in the two principal directions plus shear stresses on those planes
explain: Just as the maximum normal stress is a principal stress, the minimum normal stress at a point is also always a principal stress (the minor principal stress).

q: 20. Two bars of different materials and same size are subjected to the same tensile force. If the bars have unit elongation in the ratio of 2 : 5, then the ratio of modulus of elasticity of the two materials will be
explain: Since strain (unit elongation) is inversely proportional to E for the same stress (E=stress/strain), a strain ratio of 2:5 gives an E ratio of 5:2.

q: 21. When a bar of length l and diameter d is rigidly fixed at the upper end and hanging freely, then the total elongation produced in the bar due to its own weight is
explain: For a bar hanging under its own weight (w = weight per unit volume), the total elongation is wl²/2E, derived by integrating the varying internal axial force along the length.

q: 22. The length of a conical bar is l, diameter of base is d and weight per unit volume is w. It is fixed at its upper end and hanging freely. The elongation of the bar under the action of its own weight will be
explain: For a conical bar under self-weight, integrating gives an elongation of wl²/6E, consistent with it being one-third of the prismatic bar's wl²/2E value.

q: 23. The Poisson's ratio for cast iron varies from
explain: Cast iron typically has a somewhat higher/varying Poisson's ratio range of about 0.25 to 0.33 compared to steel.

q: 24. When a bar of length l, width b and thickness t is subjected to a push of P, its
options: length increases, width and thickness decreases
length decreases, width and thickness increases
explain: Under axial compression (a push), the bar shortens (length decreases) while it expands laterally due to Poisson's effect (width and thickness increase).

q: 25. In the case of T section, the maximum bending stress will occur at
explain: Since a T-section's neutral axis is closer to the flange, the farthest extreme fibre (in the web, at the bottom) experiences the maximum bending stress.

q: 26. Limiting values of Poisson's ratio are
explain: From thermodynamic stability requirements for isotropic elastic materials, Poisson's ratio must lie between −1 and 0.5.

q: 27. The percentage of elongation of a material with applied direct tensile test is:
explain: While percentage elongation is a measure of 'Ductility', the answer key provided marks 'Rupture' (c). In testing context, elongation is measured until the point of rupture/failure.

q: 28. If 'S' is the axial acting on an element 'ds' of a structural member with cross sectional area 'A' and modulus of elasticity 'E' the total strain energy of the member on account of axial force 'S' is given by
explain: The standard formula for axial strain energy is $U = \int  rac{P^2}{2AE} dx$.

q: 29. If the span of real beam is l, the span of the corresponding conjugate beam is
explain: In the conjugate beam method, the conjugate beam has the same span (length) as the real beam; only the support conditions and loading (M/EI diagram) change.

q: 30. The loading on the conjugate beam will be
options: loading on the real beam divided by EI
B.M. diagram divided by SF diagram
explain: The conjugate beam method loads the conjugate beam with the M/EI diagram of the real beam (bending moment diagram divided by flexural rigidity EI).

q: 31. The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
options: supporting conditions at the two ends
explain: Thermal stress develops only if expansion/contraction is restrained; hence it depends fundamentally on the support/end conditions (degree of restraint), not on length or area directly.

q: 32. The equation connection Yong's modulus (E) Poisson's (1/m) and Modulus of Rigidity (C), is
explain: The standard elastic relation connecting Young's modulus E, modulus of rigidity C(G), and Poisson's ratio (1/m) is E = 2C(1 + 1/m).

q: 33. Creep of material is the property indicated by
options: elongation of the materials caused by changes in material properties
time dependent strain of the materials
shortening caused by shrinkage of the member
decrease in volume of the materials affected by the weather conditions
explain: Creep is specifically defined as permanent deformation under a constant load over time.

q: 34. The shear center may be defined as
options: the point through which the resultant of the shear stress pass
the point about which the moment of shear flow is zero
the centre of gravity of section
explain: The shear center is the point where a load produces only bending and no torsion.

q: 35. The ratio of the area of cross section of a circular section to the area of its core is
explain: Core radius of a circle is r/4, so core area = π(r/4)² = πr²/16; ratio of total area (πr²) to core area is 16.

q: 36. When a close coiled helical spring is subjected to an axial twist, the material of the spring will be subjected to
explain: When a closed-coil spring is subjected to an axial twisting moment (about its own axis), the wire is subjected to bending stress (the roles of torsion and bending swap compared to axial loading).

q: 37. Shear strain theory for the failure of a material at elastic limit is due to
explain: The shear strain energy (distortion energy) theory of failure is attributed to Von Mises (also known as the Von Mises-Hencky theory).

q: 38. The sum of normal stress is
explain: The sum of normal stresses on two mutually perpendicular planes at a point (σx + σy) is a stress invariant — it remains constant regardless of the orientation of the planes chosen.

q: 39. The radius of Mohr's circle for two equal unlike principle stresses of magnitude P is
explain: For two equal but unlike (opposite sign) principal stresses +P and −P, the radius of Mohr's circle = (σ1−σ2)/2 = (P−(−P))/2 = P.

q: 40. At the neutral axis of a beam
options: the layers are subjected to maximum bending stress
the layers are subjected to minimum bending stress
the layers are subjected to compression
the layers do not undergo any strain
explain: Fibres along the neutral axis experience zero strain (neither elongation nor compression) during bending, by definition of the neutral axis.

q: 41. The neutral axis of a transverse section of a beam passes through the centre of gravity of the section and is
options: in the same plane in which the beam bends
at right angle to the plane in which the beam bends
explain: The neutral axis lies perpendicular to the plane of bending (the plane containing the applied loads and curvature), while passing through the section's centroid.

q: 42. In a beam subjected to pure bending, the intensity of stress in any fibre is ............. the distance of the fibre from the neutral axis.
explain: From the flexure formula σ = My/I, bending stress varies linearly (directly proportional) with distance y from the neutral axis.

q: 43. Shear center of a half circular section of radius r and a constant thickness, lies at a distance of from the center where x is
explain: For a thin semicircular section, the shear centre lies at a distance of 4r/π from the centre of the circle, a standard derived result.

q: 44. In case of eccentrically loaded struts ............. is preferred
explain: For eccentrically loaded struts, a composite section is preferred as it can be tailored (e.g., unsymmetric distribution) to better resist the resulting combined bending and axial stresses.

q: 45. The stress developed in the material without any permanent set is called
explain: The elastic limit is defined as the maximum stress up to which the material returns to its original shape completely (no permanent set) after unloading.

q: 46. The locus of the end point of the resultant of the normal and tangential components of the stress on an inclined plane is
explain: As the inclination of the plane varies, the resultant stress vector's endpoint traces out an ellipse (the stress ellipse), similar to the momental ellipse for inertia.

q: 47. Twisting moment is a moment applied in the plane of cross-section acting about
explain: Twisting (torsional) moment acts about the longitudinal axis of the member, causing rotation of cross-sections relative to each other.

q: 48. A brittle material will
options: never be used for structural purposes
explain: Brittle materials fracture suddenly with little to no prior plastic deformation or visible warning, unlike ductile materials.

q: 49. The greatest load which a spring can carry without getting permanently distorted is called
explain: Proof load is defined as the maximum load a spring can withstand without undergoing permanent deformation.

q: 50. If the Young's modulus of elasticity of a material is twice of its modulus of rigidity, the Poisson's ratio of the material is
explain: Using E = 2G(1+μ), if E = 2G, then 2G = 2G(1+μ), giving 1+μ=1, so μ = 0 (zero).

q: 51. Impact test enables to estimate the property of
explain: Impact tests (like Charpy/Izod) measure the energy absorbed during fracture, which is a direct measure of a material's toughness.

q: 52. If the Poisson's ratio of a material is 0.25, the ratio of Modulus of rigidity to the Young's Modulus is
explain: Using G/E = 1/[2(1+μ)], substituting μ=0.25 gives G/E = 1/2.5 = 0.4.

q: 53. Who introduced the terms upper and lower yield points?
explain: The terms 'upper yield point' and 'lower yield point' were introduced by Bach, based on his stress-strain testing observations.

q: 54. The shear stress at any section of a shaft is maximum
options: at the centre of the section
at a distance r/2 from the centre
at the top of the surface
at a distance 3/4r from the centre
explain: For a circular shaft under torsion, shear stress increases linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the outer surface.

q: 55. When a column is subjected to an eccentric load, the stress induced in the column will be
explain: An eccentric load on a column can be resolved into an axial load (causing direct stress) plus a moment (causing bending stress), so the combined stress includes both components.

q: 56. For no tension condition in the base of a short column of circular section, the line of action of the load should be within a circle of diameter equal to ............. of the main circle.
explain: As established (core of circular section), the no-tension zone for a circular column is a concentric circle of diameter equal to one-fourth of the main section's diameter.

q: 57. The limit of eccentricity for no tensile conditions for a column of circular section of diameter (d) is
explain: The eccentricity limit (core radius) for a circular column of diameter d is d/8 (i.e., radius r/4 = d/8), beyond which tension develops.
